title: Underwater hockey coaching, tactics, equipment, and visual-library research
scope: Verified source catalog plus original editorial seeds and conceptual diagrams. No project code, assets copied from sources, purchases, uploads, or publishing.

editorialPolicy.sourceHierarchy: Use applicable official rules for rules and equipment compliance. Use federation education for local training pathways. Label coaching ideas, research, and vendor claims separately.
editorialPolicy.copyright: These summaries, card concepts, normalized schematic layouts, and analysis workflows are original. Sources retain their own rights. No source text, photographs, paid PDFs, video files, or source diagrams should be copied into the site or GitHub repository.
editorialPolicy.licensing: No source-wide permissive license was verified. Public accessibility is not permission to mirror. Embed only using the publisher's permitted embed mechanism; prefer a direct source link when permission or playback is unclear.
editorialPolicy.safety: All in-water learning requires an appropriately supervised club or coaching setting and the applicable safety guidance. Do not train breath-hold alone, prescribe apnea duration/distance targets, hyperventilation, breath-hold contests, or urge someone to remain submerged. The separate safety research should supply authoritative safety copy.
editorialPolicy.medical: Do not turn research abstracts or historical training manuals into medical, nutrition, rehabilitation, or breath-hold prescriptions.
editorialPolicy.dates: A recent crawl is not a publication date. Display document version/date separately from checkedAt.
editorialPolicy.completeness: A broad starting library, not a claim to exhaust every country, club, vendor, video, or coaching tradition.

chapters.title: Your first session
chapters.summary: Begin with a supervised club session and borrowed kit. The first goal is to feel comfortable following the puck and returning to the surface, not to stay down longer.

sections.heading: Before the pool
sections.text: Ask the club what it lends, what swim confidence it expects, and how its beginner group is supervised. Explain equipment fit or accessibility needs early. Learn how to stop, get help, and leave the play.

sections.heading: A simple learning loop
sections.text: Watch one short demonstration, try one task, surface freely, and talk with the coach. Start with controlling and sharing the puck. Add rules and decisions in manageable pieces.

sections.heading: Signs of progress
sections.text: You can identify your team, follow the puck, use your equipment comfortably, make a controlled pass, and find another player after releasing it. These are more useful early milestones than distance or breath-hold scores.

chapters.editorialStatus: Original editorial synthesis for educational use; technical review by a qualified UWH coach recommended before public release.

chapters.title: Control the puck while seeing the game
chapters.summary: Control gives you time to choose. Build a comfortable range of puck movement, then gradually move attention from the puck toward teammates and space.

sections.heading: Practice priorities
sections.text: Begin with a movement you can repeat smoothly. Work in both directions and use an appropriate left- or right-handed stick. Add speed only after control is reliable.

sections.heading: Useful families
sections.text: Push-pull, figure patterns, direction changes, and curls train different parts of the same problem: keeping the puck available while your body and view change.

sections.heading: What a coach can observe
sections.text: Does the puck remain within usable reach? Can the player look up? Is the next movement controlled? Is the free hand staying clear of opponents? Observe quality before increasing pressure.

chapters.editorialStatus: Original editorial synthesis for educational use; technical review by a qualified UWH coach recommended before public release.

chapters.title: Passing and receiving as one action
chapters.summary: A pass succeeds when a teammate can use it. Choose the route, receiver, and next support position together.

sections.heading: Choose the useful pass
sections.text: A flat pass and a lifted flick solve different spatial problems. Begin with accuracy in a clear lane. More distance or height is not automatically better, and an unsafe trajectory is never the objective.

sections.heading: Receiver and passer
sections.text: The receiver offers a visible target and prepares for the next action. The passer follows the release by moving into useful space. A completed pass should improve the team's options.

sections.heading: Coaching questions
sections.text: Was the lane open? Was the receiver ready? Could a shorter or sideways pass have preserved possession? For flick mechanics, use a qualified coach and the linked demonstrations rather than copying a still picture.

chapters.editorialStatus: Original editorial synthesis for educational use; technical review by a qualified UWH coach recommended before public release.

chapters.title: The strike is a decision point
chapters.summary: Reaching the puck first creates an opportunity. What happens next depends on support, opponent shape, and available space.

sections.heading: Look beyond the puck
sections.text: A supporting teammate may be beside or behind the first player. The first touch should connect with that support rather than blindly sending the puck forward.

sections.heading: Two pictures to review
sections.text: Freeze video before the first touch to identify the support options. Then freeze after the first exchange to see which team has a playable next action.

sections.heading: Rule boundary
sections.text: This is a tactical discussion. Starting positions, permitted entry, and restart procedure come from the applicable current rules, not an old coaching clip.

chapters.editorialStatus: Original editorial synthesis for educational use; technical review by a qualified UWH coach recommended before public release.

chapters.title: Width, depth, and a playable next option
chapters.summary: Support means being reachable and useful. A teammate directly beside the puck may still be unavailable if the passing lane is crowded.

sections.heading: The support picture
sections.text: Think of the puck carrier, a reachable teammate, and space for the next action. Change the shape as the puck moves. Spacing should create options without disconnecting the team.

sections.heading: After releasing the puck
sections.text: Reposition rather than admiring the pass. The next useful position could be behind, beside, or ahead of play. The correct choice changes with possession and pressure.

sections.heading: Availability is dynamic
sections.text: Players surface whenever needed. Teammates can read who is available and fill a useful role; tactical structure must never pressure someone to extend a breath hold.

chapters.editorialStatus: Original editorial synthesis for educational use; technical review by a qualified UWH coach recommended before public release.

chapters.title: Formation shapes are shared reference points
chapters.summary: Read underwater-hockey formation numbers from the attacking line toward the defensive line. The same shape can use different role names and play differently in different clubs.

sections.heading: Choose a common language
sections.text: Agree which end is being attacked and what words the team uses for forward, wing, center, back, and stopper. A formation label alone does not explain responsibilities.

sections.heading: Use shapes to ask questions
sections.text: Who offers the first pass? Who covers behind an engagement? Who protects the opposite side? What changes when possession turns over? Ask these questions for each shape.

sections.heading: Avoid false certainty
sections.text: No diagram guarantees success. Actual positions change with the puck, wall, available players, and opposition. The examples below are original schematic layouts, not mandatory or optimal positions.

chapters.editorialStatus: Original editorial synthesis for educational use; technical review by a qualified UWH coach recommended before public release.

chapters.title: React together when possession changes
chapters.summary: A turnover changes which spaces are useful. The nearest player and the covering players have different jobs.

sections.heading: Three observations
sections.text: Locate the puck, identify immediate pressure, and look for uncovered space. Avoid having every player pursue the same contest.

sections.heading: Cover behind pressure
sections.text: When one player engages, another can remain available behind the play. On regaining possession, look for a controlled exit that teammates can support.

sections.heading: Training question
sections.text: Pause a small-sided game at a turnover. Ask each player to name their next job and show one alternative. Replay the same starting picture with a different response.

chapters.editorialStatus: Original editorial synthesis for educational use; technical review by a qualified UWH coach recommended before public release.

chapters.title: Use small games to connect technique and decisions
chapters.summary: An isolated movement becomes useful when a player recognizes when to use it. Small-sided games connect that movement to a teammate, opponent, and purpose.

sections.heading: Change one constraint
sections.text: A coach can change playing space, available teammates, the scoring target, or defender pressure. Change one variable at a time so players can understand what helped.

sections.heading: Choose an observable
sections.text: Look for a behavior such as offering a passing option, receiving under control, or supporting after release. Avoid judging the entire exercise only by goals.

sections.heading: Keep the task playable
sections.text: If the challenge overwhelms the skill, simplify it. If the task is easy, add one decision. Rest, surface access, and supervision are prerequisites, not rewards for success.

chapters.editorialStatus: Original editorial synthesis for educational use; technical review by a qualified UWH coach recommended before public release.

chapters.title: Watch one question at a time
chapters.summary: A useful review starts with a question. For example: after we pass, do we still have a reachable support player?

sections.heading: An original review workflow
sections.text: Choose a short sequence. Watch once at normal speed, then pause before the key decision. Record what was visible, the option taken, and the outcome. Look for another comparable sequence before drawing conclusions.

sections.heading: A compact tagging sheet
sections.text: Timestamp; phase; possession; pool zone; number of visible support options; chosen action; outcome; one question for training. Mark unclear views as unknown rather than assigning blame.

sections.heading: From footage to practice
sections.text: Pick one team behavior to test next session. Review both successful and unsuccessful examples. Camera angle and missing off-screen players can change the interpretation.

sections.heading: Rights and consent
sections.text: Link public broadcasts at their original publisher. Use team footage only with appropriate permission, particularly where children are involved. Do not rehost or publish identifiable coaching clips by default.

chapters.editorialStatus: Original editorial synthesis for educational use; technical review by a qualified UWH coach recommended before public release.

chapters.title: Choose kit by fit, function, and the current rules
chapters.summary: Borrow and compare before buying. A comfortable legal setup that works together is more useful than selecting each item from a brand ranking.

sections.heading: Personal fit
sections.text: Check mask seal and field of view, snorkel and mouthguard compatibility, cap and ear protection, fin-pocket comfort, and a glove that lets you grip the stick securely.

sections.heading: Playing preference
sections.text: Stick shape and handedness affect feel. Fin stiffness and length affect comfort and maneuvering; test with a coach rather than assuming harder or more expensive means better.

sections.heading: Before a competition
sections.text: Check the actual tournament rules and equipment inspection. Product marketing and a club's old gear page do not establish legal compliance.

sections.heading: Buying across borders
sections.text: Compare the full landed cost, available sizes, return policy, lead time, and replacement parts. Ask whether a club order can reduce shipping; never assume a directory's old shipping offer still applies.

chapters.editorialStatus: Original editorial synthesis for educational use; technical review by a qualified UWH coach recommended before public release.

chapters.title: Inspect, rinse, dry, and replace
chapters.summary: A simple gear check prevents avoidable session interruptions. Follow the maker's care instructions for each material.

sections.heading: Before play
sections.text: Inspect straps, mask lenses, cap ear guards, fin edges, glove padding, and stick surfaces. Remove damaged or sharp equipment from use and have a knowledgeable club member assess it.

sections.heading: After play
sections.text: Rinse and dry gear as its manufacturer recommends. Keep personal and club-loan equipment identifiable. For shared mouth-contact equipment, follow the club's hygiene procedure.

sections.heading: Keep a repair log
sections.text: For club equipment, record defects and who checked them. Separate serviceable items from those awaiting repair. Replacement decisions should prioritize safe function.

chapters.editorialStatus: Original editorial synthesis for educational use; technical review by a qualified UWH coach recommended before public release.

chapters.title: DIY belongs inside a safety and compliance check
chapters.summary: Homemade gloves and sticks are part of the sport's history. A homemade item still needs to protect people, avoid damage, and satisfy current competition requirements.

sections.heading: Reasonable scope
sections.text: Start with non-safety-critical organizational aids such as equipment labels, storage dividers, and dryland tactics boards. Discuss any playing-equipment project with an experienced club maker.

sections.heading: Gloves and sticks
sections.text: Use appropriate materials, maker instructions, curing conditions, and a post-build inspection. Do not infer that a material is safe on skin simply because a historical tutorial used it.

sections.heading: Leave high-risk systems to specialists
sections.text: This atlas does not provide lead-smelting, underwater electrical-buzzer, or load-bearing goal-construction instructions. Pool operators and qualified specialists should approve systems used in the pool.

chapters.editorialStatus: Original editorial synthesis for educational use; technical review by a qualified UWH coach recommended before public release.

chapters.title: Coaching qualifications and learning are different layers
chapters.summary: Technical knowledge is one part of coaching. Qualification systems also address safe delivery, welfare, planning, assessment, and responsibilities.

sections.heading: Start with your federation
sections.text: Use the pathway that applies in your country and club. Confirm admission criteria, safeguarding checks, first-aid expectations, and how the practical assessment works.

sections.heading: Learn from other countries
sections.text: Foreign manuals can offer useful perspectives on technique or pedagogy. They do not automatically authorize coaching locally or establish equivalent qualifications.

sections.heading: Make the next session better
sections.text: Choose one learning objective, explain the task clearly, observe a behavior, and adapt. Invite player feedback and keep selection and playing-time decisions transparent.

chapters.title: Read the source labels before using a resource
chapters.summary: A page being online today does not mean its contents are current. A free download is not necessarily free to republish.

sections.heading: Four useful distinctions
sections.text: Official rule; federation education; club/coaching opinion; commercial material. Each can help, but they answer different questions.

sections.heading: Check the document itself
sections.text: Read its edition and publication date. Search-engine crawl dates describe indexing, not authorship. Mark an older source as historical when rule or safety guidance may have changed.

sections.heading: Respect the author's work
sections.text: Use short original summaries with direct links. Keep photographs, diagrams, paid manuals, and videos at their original publisher unless a clear license or permission allows reuse.

chapters.editorialStatus: Original editorial synthesis for educational use; technical review by a qualified UWH coach recommended before public release.

practiceCards.title: Control and look up
practiceCards.players: One active player per safe station, with required supervision
practiceCards.concept: Move the puck between a few comfortable target areas. A coach presents a simple visual cue to encourage looking ahead. Simplify the movement when control breaks down.
observe: Head lifts without loss of control
practiceCards.adapt: Begin with fewer target areas; add a choice only when ready.
practiceCards.safety: In-water tasks require appropriate qualified supervision, safe spacing, unrestricted surfacing, and adaptation to the group. This card sets no breath-hold target.

practiceCards.title: Pass and offer support
practiceCards.purpose: Make support the action after a pass
practiceCards.players: Two active players in a supervised club session
practiceCards.concept: A pair exchanges a controlled pass. The passer changes position and offers a visible next option. Stop and discuss whether the lane was clear and the receiver was ready.
practiceCards.adapt: Reduce movement first; later let the receiver choose the next target.
practiceCards.safety: In-water tasks require appropriate qualified supervision, safe spacing, unrestricted surfacing, and adaptation to the group. This card sets no breath-hold target.

practiceCards.title: Read a two-versus-one
practiceCards.purpose: Choose between carrying and sharing the puck
practiceCards.players: Two attackers, one defender, qualified supervision
practiceCards.concept: Begin from a coach-selected open picture. The attackers try to reach a target area through legal play. Reset to compare a passing option with a carrying option.
practiceCards.adapt: Use passive defensive pressure first, or more space; increase difficulty only when appropriate.
practiceCards.safety: In-water tasks require appropriate qualified supervision, safe spacing, unrestricted surfacing, and adaptation to the group. This card sets no breath-hold target.

practiceCards.title: Pause at the turnover
practiceCards.concept: After a change of possession, stop safely on the agreed signal. Ask each player to identify the puck, the immediate threat, and their next useful role. Replay the starting picture.
practiceCards.adapt: Start with fewer players and a clear possession change.
practiceCards.safety: In-water tasks require appropriate qualified supervision, safe spacing, unrestricted surfacing, and adaptation to the group. This card sets no breath-hold target.

practiceCards.title: Three-frame video review
practiceCards.purpose: Connect observation to a practice question
practiceCards.concept: Select before-decision, action, and outcome frames. Each viewer names one visible option before hearing the result. Record unknowns caused by the camera angle.
practiceCards.adapt: Choose a simple pass first; later compare several similar possessions.
practiceCards.safety: In-water tasks require appropriate qualified supervision, safe spacing, unrestricted surfacing, and adaptation to the group. This card sets no breath-hold target.

practiceCards.title: Move a formation on a tactics board
practiceCards.purpose: Agree role vocabulary without breath-hold pressure
equipment: Tactics board or original interactive pool diagram
practiceCards.concept: Place six markers in a chosen reference shape. Move the puck to a side, then reverse possession. Ask who supports, who covers, and which positions change.
observe: Players use the same role names
practiceCards.adapt: Compare two shapes without declaring either universally better.
practiceCards.safety: In-water tasks require appropriate qualified supervision, safe spacing, unrestricted surfacing, and adaptation to the group. This card sets no breath-hold target.

practiceCards.title: Compare borrowed kit
practiceCards.purpose: Find a comfortable starting setup before spending
practiceCards.concept: Check one item's fit and compatibility at a time. Record which setup was comfortable and which caused leaks, rubbing, or insecure grip. Confirm rules before purchase.
practiceCards.adapt: Prioritize available loan equipment and budget before specialized upgrades.
practiceCards.safety: In-water tasks require appropriate qualified supervision, safe spacing, unrestricted surfacing, and adaptation to the group. This card sets no breath-hold target.

practiceCards.title: Change one constraint
practiceCards.concept: Write one observable behavior. Choose a task, then plan one easier and one harder version by changing only space, pressure, or available support. Ask players what they noticed.
practiceCards.adapt: Seek a mentor's review when using unfamiliar tasks.
practiceCards.safety: In-water tasks require appropriate qualified supervision, safe spacing, unrestricted surfacing, and adaptation to the group. This card sets no breath-hold target.

qualityFlags.detail: The same Level-2 Block-5 URL is indexed as Support & Connection but directly opens as Formation Under Pressure (2-3-1). Exact current revision is unresolved. Publish original independently reviewed concepts, link the source with a snapshot warning, and avoid implying the wiki has one stable curriculum.

German community training PDF at https://uwsport.de/files/0904%20-%20uwh_training.pdf explicitly encourages approaching breath-hold limits and suppressing the breathing stimulus. Exclude as training guidance. It is not included in the public source catalog.

qualityFlags.topic: Do not treat old manuals as current rulebooks
qualityFlags.detail: WUHA manual is June 1999 rev 2. Italian manual is 16 March 2015 ed 1.0. Fresh indexing does not update either document.
Some club pages call mouthguards optional or give old mask/glove restrictions. Current official/event equipment rules override these pages; do not copy their compliance claims.
Root URL timed out, although multiple deep pages are indexed. 1-3-2 page explicitly has video placeholders. Distinguish indexed text from tested media.
Equipment-guide and February 2025 rule download links redirect to login. Link hub and disclose access; do not claim the download was inspected.
TUHA calls CanAm Canadian; another club calls it US. Use North America until legal storefront location is independently verified.
Do not repeat 'best performance', universal fin recommendations, old shipping offers, or directory price estimates as independent conclusions.

This coaching-specific library covers English, French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Turkish, and German resources. Asia/Africa technical material remains less well represented; do not mistake that retrieval gap for absence of local coaching.
FPAS course platform returned a browser challenge, FVAS course failed direct fetch, BOA intro page requires login. Public overviews may still be useful.

validation.caution: Verification records distinguish opened text, indexed-only text, login gates, errors, and outbound links. A loaded URL does not validate every claim on the page.
